Pseudobulk differential expression with DESeq2

Local version, reads from the workshop data repo, no network access

Published

August 4, 2026

ImportantRead this before you trust anything below

This document is a transcription of the upstream HBC lesson Single-cell RNA-seq: Pseudobulk differential expression analysis (https://hbctraining.github.io/scRNA-seq/lessons/pseudobulk_DESeq2_scrnaseq.html), adapted only so that it reads its input from the workshop data repo instead of a downloaded data/ folder.

The document renders end to end. Two chunks fail on purpose and are recovered by a fallback in the very next chunk, so the rendered page shows exactly two error blocks and then keeps going.

The upstream page carries an ARCHIVED banner and the lesson script is dated May 2020. Expect API drift against current DESeq2, Seurat, and scater. Two calls are known to be affected. scater::calculateQCMetrics() is now defunct, and Matrix.utils was archived on CRAN so aggregate.Matrix() is unavailable. Both are transcribed as the tutorial has them, each followed by a modern equivalent. The document sets error: false, so any unexpected failure stops the render and is reported. These two chunks, qc-tutorial and aggregate-tutorial, carry a chunk-level error: true because their failure is the point being taught.

Learning objectives

  • Understand how to prepare single-cell RNA-seq raw count data for pseudobulk differential expression analysis.
  • Use DESeq2 to perform pseudobulk differential expression analysis on a specific cell type cluster.
  • Create functions to iterate the pseudobulk differential expression analysis across different cell types.

Differential expression analysis with DESeq2

After identifying the cell type identities of the scRNA-seq clusters, we often want to perform differential expression analysis between conditions within particular cell types. Functions exist within Seurat to do this, but the p-values are often inflated because each cell is treated as a sample. Single cells within a sample are not independent of each other. If we treat cells as samples we are investigating variation within an individual, not variation across a population.

The current best practice is a pseudobulk approach:

  1. Subset to the cells for the cell type(s) of interest.
  2. Extract the raw counts after QC filtering.
  3. Aggregate the counts and metadata to the sample level.
  4. Perform the DE analysis. At least two biological replicates per condition are required, and more are recommended.

Setting up the R environment

source(here::here("slides", "find_data_dir.R"))
data_dir <- find_data_dir("2_a_pseudobulk_de")
report_data_dir("2_a_pseudobulk_de")

Where the data came from

Upstream tells students to right-click and download the RDS object into a data/ folder. The verbatim download link on the lesson page is:

https://www.dropbox.com/s/dgdooocb1a03dvk/scRNA-seq_input_data_for_DE.rds?dl=1

For the workshop that file is already staged, so the chunks below read it from data_dir and never touch the network.

Load libraries

# May 2020
# Single-cell RNA-seq analysis - Pseudobulk DE analysis with DESeq2

# Load libraries
library(scater)
library(Seurat)
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
# library(Matrix.utils)  # archived on CRAN; not loaded. See the aggregation
#                        # section, which shows aggregate.Matrix() failing and
#                        # uses a Matrix-only replacement instead.
library(edgeR)
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)
library(Matrix)
library(purrr)
library(reshape2)
library(S4Vectors)
library(tibble)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(pheatmap)
library(apeglm)
library(png)
library(DESeq2)
library(RColorBrewer)

Deriving the aggregation metadata

ImportantThe staged object is the raw Kang object, so we build the three key columns here

The upstream lesson assumes sce already carries cluster_id, sample_id, and group_id. The object distributed for this workshop is the raw Kang et al. 2017 SingleCellExperiment, whose colData instead has cell (cell type), ind (individual), and stim (condition). We derive the three columns the tutorial needs, exactly as muscat::prepSCE() would: cluster_id from the cell type, group_id from the condition, and sample_id from condition plus individual (so ctrl and individual 101 give sample ctrl101). Without this step every chunk below fails, because sce$cluster_id and friends are NULL.

# Drop the handful of cells with no cell-type assignment.
sce <- sce[, !is.na(sce$cell)]

sce$cluster_id <- factor(sce$cell)
sce$group_id   <- factor(sce$stim)
sce$sample_id  <- factor(paste0(sce$stim, sce$ind))

head(colData(sce)[, c("cluster_id", "sample_id", "group_id")])

Acquiring necessary metrics for aggregation across cells in a sample

# Named vector of cluster names
kids <- purrr::set_names(levels(sce$cluster_id))
kids

          "B cells"   "CD14+ Monocytes"       "CD4 T cells"       "CD8 T cells" 
    Dendritic cells   FCGR3A+ Monocytes      Megakaryocytes            NK cells

# Total number of clusters
nk <- length(kids)

# Named vector of sample names
sids <- purrr::set_names(levels(sce$sample_id))

# Total number of samples
ns <- length(sids)
ns
[1] 16

To perform sample-level DE we need sample-level metadata. We reorder the single-cell metadata to match the order of the sample ID factor levels, then take the sample-level information from the first cell of each sample.

# Generate sample level metadata

## Determine the number of cells per sample
table(sce$sample_id)

 ctrl101 ctrl1015 ctrl1016 ctrl1039  ctrl107 ctrl1244 ctrl1256 ctrl1488 
    1027     3138     2180      551      645     2250     2451     2375 
 stim101 stim1015 stim1016 stim1039  stim107 stim1244 stim1256 stim1488 
    1363     2703     1998      791      641     1755     2274     2914 
## Turn named vector into a numeric vector of number of cells per sample
n_cells <- as.numeric(table(sce$sample_id))

## Determine how to reorder the samples (rows) of the metadata to match the
## order of sample names in the sids vector
m <- match(sids, sce$sample_id)

## Create the sample level metadata by combining the reordered metadata with
## the number of cells corresponding to each sample.
ei <- data.frame(colData(sce)[m, ],
                 n_cells, row.names = NULL) %>%
  dplyr::select(-"cluster_id")
ei

Quality control

Upstream removes count outliers and low count genes with scater, following the 2019 Bioconductor tutorial. A real analysis would do a more careful and more hands-on job of QC.

# Perform QC if not already performed
dim(sce)
[1] 35635 29056
# Calculate quality control (QC) metrics. This is the upstream call, and it fails
# on purpose: calculateQCMetrics() is defunct in current scater. The next chunk
# computes the same is_outlier flag with scuttle, the modern equivalent.
sce <- calculateQCMetrics(sce)
Error in `calculateQCMetrics()`:
! 'calculateQCMetrics' is defunct.
Use 'perCellQCMetrics' instead.
See help("Defunct")
WarningcalculateQCMetrics() was removed from scater

scater::calculateQCMetrics() and the total_features_by_counts column it created were deprecated in Bioconductor 3.10 and removed after that. The modern equivalent lives in scuttle, where the per-cell count of detected genes is called detected. The chunk below computes sce$is_outlier the modern way, but only if the tutorial chunk above failed to create it, so the tutorial code stays authoritative when it happens to work.

if (is.null(sce$is_outlier)) {
  message("calculateQCMetrics() did not run. Using scuttle::perCellQCMetrics().")
  qc <- scuttle::perCellQCMetrics(sce)
  sce$total_features_by_counts <- qc$detected
  sce$is_outlier <- scuttle::isOutlier(
    metric = qc$detected,
    nmads = 2, type = "both", log = TRUE)
}
table(sce$is_outlier)

FALSE  TRUE 
26828  2228 
# Remove outlier cells
sce <- sce[, !sce$is_outlier]
dim(sce)
[1] 35635 26828
## Remove lowly expressed genes which have less than 10 cells with any counts
sce <- sce[rowSums(counts(sce) > 1) >= 10, ]

dim(sce)
[1]  7120 26828

Count aggregation to sample level

We take the sum of counts for each sample within each cell type.

# Aggregate the counts per sample_id and cluster_id

# Subset metadata to only include the cluster and sample IDs to aggregate across
groups <- colData(sce)[, c("cluster_id", "sample_id")]

# Aggregate across cluster-sample groups. This is the upstream call, and it fails
# on purpose: aggregate.Matrix() lived in the archived Matrix.utils. The
# Matrix-only replacement two chunks down produces the same sums, and the chunk
# after it inspects the result.
pb <- aggregate.Matrix(t(counts(sce)),
                       groupings = groups, fun = "sum")
Error in `aggregate.Matrix()`:
! could not find function "aggregate.Matrix"
ImportantMatrix.utils is archived on CRAN

Matrix.utils was archived on CRAN in 2020, so aggregate.Matrix() may simply not be installable on a current R. The commented-out chunk below does the same sum-by-group using only Matrix, which is a base recommended package. A sparse model matrix of group indicators, crossproduct with the cell-by-gene matrix, gives exactly the group-by-gene sums that aggregate.Matrix(fun = "sum") returns, with the same cluster_sample row names.

The chunk after it runs that fallback for real, but only when pb does not already exist, so the document can carry on to DESeq2 either way.

# # Matrix-only replacement for Matrix.utils::aggregate.Matrix(fun = "sum")
#
# group_key <- factor(paste(colData(sce)$cluster_id,
#                           colData(sce)$sample_id,
#                           sep = "_"))
#
# # One indicator column per cluster-sample group, cells in rows.
# mm <- Matrix::sparse.model.matrix(~ 0 + group_key)
# colnames(mm) <- levels(group_key)
#
# # crossprod(mm, cells_by_genes) sums each gene over the cells of each group.
# pb <- Matrix::crossprod(mm, Matrix::t(counts(sce)))
if (!exists("pb")) {
  message("aggregate.Matrix() unavailable. Using the Matrix-only fallback.")
  group_key <- factor(paste(colData(sce)$cluster_id,
                            colData(sce)$sample_id,
                            sep = "_"))
  mm <- Matrix::sparse.model.matrix(~ 0 + group_key)
  colnames(mm) <- levels(group_key)
  pb <- Matrix::crossprod(mm, Matrix::t(counts(sce)))
}

The output is a sparse matrix with cell type-sample rows and gene columns. For example, within B cells, sample ctrl101 has a count for gene NOC2L.

To run DE per cell type we need to split the data by cell type, and transpose each piece so that genes are rows and samples are columns. Not every sample contains cells of every cell type, so we first work out which rows belong to which cluster.

# Not every cluster is present in all samples; create a vector that represents
# how to split samples
splitf <- sapply(stringr::str_split(rownames(pb),
                                    pattern = "_",
                                    n = 2),
                 `[`, 1)

# Turn into a list and split the list into components for each cluster and
# transform, so rows are genes and columns are samples and make rownames as the
# sample IDs
pb <- split.data.frame(pb,
                       factor(splitf)) %>%
  lapply(function(u)
    set_colnames(t(u),
                 stringr::str_extract(rownames(u), "(?<=_)[:alnum:]+")))

Differential gene expression with DESeq2

DESeq2 normalizes the count data to account for differences in library size and RNA composition between samples. We then use the normalized counts for QC plots at the gene and sample level, and finally run the differential expression test.

Sample-level metadata

We need metadata for all samples, including cluster ID, sample ID, and the condition of interest (group_id), plus any other sample-level metadata such as batch, sex, or age. ei holds the sample ID and condition, so we combine it with the cluster IDs.

# Get sample names for each of the cell type clusters

# prep. data.frame for plotting
get_sample_ids <- function(x) {
  pb[[x]] %>%
    colnames()
}

de_samples <- map(1:length(kids), get_sample_ids) %>%
  unlist()
# Get cluster IDs for each of the samples

samples_list <- map(1:length(kids), get_sample_ids)

get_cluster_ids <- function(x) {
  rep(names(pb)[x],
      each = length(samples_list[[x]]))
}

de_cluster_ids <- map(1:length(kids), get_cluster_ids) %>%
  unlist()
# Create a data frame with the sample IDs, cluster IDs and condition

gg_df <- data.frame(cluster_id = de_cluster_ids,
                    sample_id = de_samples)

gg_df <- left_join(gg_df, ei[, c("sample_id", "group_id")])

metadata <- gg_df %>%
  dplyr::select(cluster_id, sample_id, group_id)

Subsetting dataset to cluster(s) of interest

# Generate vector of cluster IDs
clusters <- levels(factor(metadata$cluster_id))
clusters
[1] "B cells"           "CD14+ Monocytes"   "CD4 T cells"       "CD8 T cells"      
[5] "Dendritic cells"   "FCGR3A+ Monocytes" "Megakaryocytes"    "NK cells"
Note

Upstream writes clusters <- levels(metadata$cluster_id). Since R 4.0, data.frame() defaults to stringsAsFactors = FALSE, so metadata$cluster_id is a character vector and levels() on it returns NULL. That would silently make clusters empty and break every chunk below. Wrapping it in factor() restores the intent of the original.

We run the DE analysis on B cells, the first element of the vector.

group_id has to be a factor for the levels() calls in the contrast code below to work, so we make sure of that here.

cluster_metadata$group_id <- factor(cluster_metadata$group_id)
levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)
[1] "ctrl" "stim"

Create DESeq2 object

The design formula should also include any other metadata columns whose variation we want to regress out, for example batch, sex, or age. Here we only have the comparison of interest, group_id.

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cluster_counts,
                              colData = cluster_metadata,
                              design = ~ group_id)
dds

dim: 7120 16 
metadata(1): version
assays(1): counts
rownames(7120): NOC2L HES4 ... S100B PRMT2
rowData names(0):
colnames(16): ctrl101 ctrl1015 ... stim1256 stim1488
colData names(3): cluster_id sample_id group_id

Quality control, sample level

Normalization and log2 transformation improve the distances used by unsupervised clustering. DESeq2 uses the median of ratios method for normalization and a regularized log transform (rlog) for sample-level QC, since it moderates the variance across the mean.

Note

The DESeq2 vignette suggests that large datasets, hundreds of samples, use the variance stabilizing transformation vst() instead of rlog(), since rlog() can be slow. With 16 samples here, rlog() is fine.

Principal component analysis

# Transform counts for data visualization
rld <- rlog(dds, blind = TRUE)

# Plot PCA
DESeq2::plotPCA(rld, intgroup = "group_id")

We expect a clean separation on PC1 by condition, which would say that the condition of interest is the largest source of variation in the dataset.

Hierarchical clustering

The heatmap shows the correlation of gene expression for all pairwise combinations of samples. Most genes are not differentially expressed, so samples generally correlate above 0.80. Values below 0.80 may flag an outlier or sample contamination.

# Extract the rlog matrix from the object and compute pairwise correlation values
rld_mat <- assay(rld)
rld_cor <- cor(rld_mat)

# Plot heatmap
pheatmap(rld_cor, annotation = cluster_metadata[, c("group_id"), drop = FALSE])

Running DESeq2

DESeq2 models the raw counts using size factors to account for differences in library depth, estimates gene-wise dispersions and shrinks them, then fits the negative binomial model and tests with the Wald test or the likelihood ratio test. All of that happens inside the single DESeq() call.

# Run DESeq2 differential expression analysis
dds <- DESeq(dds)
# Plot dispersion estimates
plotDispEsts(dds)

Dispersions should decrease with increasing mean and follow the line of best fit.

Results

We compare the stimulated group relative to the control.

# Output results of Wald test for contrast for stim vs ctrl
levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[2]
[1] "stim"
levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[1]
[1] "ctrl"
contrast <- c("group_id", levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[2], levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[1])

# resultsNames(dds)
res <- results(dds,
               contrast = contrast,
               alpha = 0.05)

res <- lfcShrink(dds,
                 contrast = contrast,
                 res = res,
                 type = "normal")
res

Note

Current DESeq2 defaults lfcShrink() to type = "apeglm", which shrinks a single coef and rejects a contrast = argument. Upstream relied on the older default of type = "normal", so we now pass type = "normal" explicitly. The alternative, type = "apeglm" with coef = resultsNames(dds)[2], is the modern recommendation but changes the reported fold changes.

We will write out the significant genes and make a few plots.

  • Table of results for all genes.
  • Table of results for significant genes, adjusted p below 0.05.
  • Scatterplot of normalized expression of the top 20 most significant genes.
  • Heatmap of all significant genes.
  • Volcano plot of results.

The tutorial writes CSV files into a results/ folder that it assumes you created by hand when you set up the project, so we create it here.

results_dir <- here::here("slides", "wed_morning", "wed_morn_tutorials", "results")
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

Upstream builds this filename from levels(cluster_metadata$sample)[2]. There is no sample column, only sample_id, so that expression is NULL and paste0() drops it, producing a file named B cells__vs__all_genes.csv with the condition names missing. We use group_id instead, which is what was meant. Upstream’s significant-genes call has a second typo on the same line, paste0("results", ...) with no trailing slash, which writes into the working directory rather than into results/. Both are fixed here.

Scatterplot of normalized expression of top 20 most significant genes

This plot is a good check that we are reading the fold change direction correctly.

## ggplot of top genes
normalized_counts <- counts(dds,
                            normalized = TRUE)

## Order results by padj values
top20_sig_genes <- sig_res %>%
  dplyr::arrange(padj) %>%
  dplyr::pull(gene) %>%
  head(n = 20)

top20_sig_norm <- data.frame(normalized_counts) %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>%
  dplyr::filter(gene %in% top20_sig_genes)

gathered_top20_sig <- top20_sig_norm %>%
  gather(colnames(top20_sig_norm)[2:length(colnames(top20_sig_norm))],
         key = "samplename", value = "normalized_counts")

gathered_top20_sig <- inner_join(ei[, c("sample_id", "group_id")],
                                 gathered_top20_sig,
                                 by = c("sample_id" = "samplename"))

## plot using ggplot2
ggplot(gathered_top20_sig) +
  geom_point(aes(x = gene,
                 y = normalized_counts,
                 color = group_id),
             position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  xlab("Genes") +
  ylab("log10 Normalized Counts") +
  ggtitle("Top 20 Significant DE Genes") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

Heatmap of all significant genes

# Extract normalized counts for only the significant genes
sig_norm <- data.frame(normalized_counts) %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>%
  dplyr::filter(gene %in% sig_res$gene)

# Set a color palette
heat_colors <- brewer.pal(6, "YlOrRd")

# Run pheatmap using the metadata data frame for the annotation
pheatmap(sig_norm[, 2:length(colnames(sig_norm))],
         color = heat_colors,
         cluster_rows = TRUE,
         show_rownames = FALSE,
         annotation = cluster_metadata[, c("group_id", "cluster_id")],

         scale = "row",

Volcano plot of results

## Obtain logical vector where TRUE values denote padj values < 0.05 and fold
## change > 1.5 in either direction
res_table_thres <- res_tbl %>%
  mutate(threshold = padj < 0.05 & abs(log2FoldChange) >= 0.58)

## Volcano plot
ggplot(res_table_thres) +
  geom_point(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), colour = threshold)) +
  ggtitle("Volcano plot of stimulated B cells relative to control") +
  xlab("log2 fold change") +
  ylab("-log10 adjusted p-value") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 50)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.5), hjust = 0.5),
        axis.title = element_text(size = rel(1.25)))

Useful scripts for running analyses on many different cell type clusters

Script to run DESeq2 on all cell type clusters, Wald test

This runs DESeq2 on every cell type cluster, contrasting one level of the condition of interest against another with the Wald test. Upstream writes its output into DESeq2/pairwise/, and we keep that layout underneath results_dir.

dir.create(file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2"), showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "pairwise"), showWarnings = FALSE)

# Function to run DESeq2 and get results for all clusters
## x is index of cluster in clusters vector on which to run function
## A is the sample group to compare
## B is the sample group to compare against (base level)

get_dds_resultsAvsB <- function(x, A, B) {
  cluster_metadata <- metadata[which(metadata$cluster_id == clusters[x]), ]
  rownames(cluster_metadata) <- cluster_metadata$sample_id
  cluster_metadata$group_id <- factor(cluster_metadata$group_id)
  counts <- pb[[clusters[x]]]
  cluster_counts <- data.frame(counts[, which(colnames(counts) %in% rownames(cluster_metadata))])

  # all(rownames(cluster_metadata) == colnames(cluster_counts))

  dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cluster_counts,
                                colData = cluster_metadata,
                                design = ~ group_id)

  # Transform counts for data visualization
  rld <- rlog(dds, blind = TRUE)

  # Plot PCA
  DESeq2::plotPCA(rld, intgroup = "group_id")
  ggsave(file.path(results_dir, paste0(clusters[x], "_specific_PCAplot.png")))

  # Extract the rlog matrix from the object and compute pairwise correlation values
  rld_mat <- assay(rld)
  rld_cor <- cor(rld_mat)

  # Plot heatmap
  png(file.path(results_dir, paste0(clusters[x], "_specific_heatmap.png")))
  pheatmap(rld_cor, annotation = cluster_metadata[, c("group_id"), drop = FALSE])
  dev.off()

  # Run DESeq2 differential expression analysis
  dds <- DESeq(dds)

  # Plot dispersion estimates
  png(file.path(results_dir, paste0(clusters[x], "_dispersion_plot.png")))
  plotDispEsts(dds)
  dev.off()

  # Output results of Wald test for contrast for A vs B
  contrast <- c("group_id", levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[A], levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[B])

  # resultsNames(dds)
  res <- results(dds,
                 contrast = contrast,
                 alpha = 0.05)

  res <- lfcShrink(dds,
                   contrast = contrast,
                   res = res,
                   type = "normal")
  # Set thresholds
  padj_cutoff <- 0.05

  # Turn the results object into a tibble for use with tidyverse functions
  res_tbl <- res %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>%
    as_tibble()

  write.csv(res_tbl,
            file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "pairwise",
                      paste0(clusters[x], "_",
                             levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[A], "_vs_",
                             levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[B],
                             "_all_genes.csv")),
            quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)

  # Subset the significant results
  sig_res <- dplyr::filter(res_tbl, padj < padj_cutoff) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(padj)

  write.csv(sig_res,
            file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "pairwise",
                      paste0(clusters[x], "_",
                             levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[A], "_vs_",
                             levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[B],
                             "_sig_genes.csv")),
            quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)

  ## ggplot of top genes
  normalized_counts <- counts(dds,
                              normalized = TRUE)

  ## Order results by padj values
  top20_sig_genes <- sig_res %>%
    dplyr::arrange(padj) %>%
    dplyr::pull(gene) %>%
    head(n = 20)

  top20_sig_norm <- data.frame(normalized_counts) %>%
    rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>%
    dplyr::filter(gene %in% top20_sig_genes)

  gathered_top20_sig <- top20_sig_norm %>%
    gather(colnames(top20_sig_norm)[2:length(colnames(top20_sig_norm))],
           key = "samplename", value = "normalized_counts")

  gathered_top20_sig <- inner_join(ei[, c("sample_id", "group_id")],
                                   gathered_top20_sig,
                                   by = c("sample_id" = "samplename"))

  ## plot using ggplot2
  ggplot(gathered_top20_sig) +
    geom_point(aes(x = gene,
                   y = normalized_counts,
                   color = group_id),
               position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    xlab("Genes") +
    ylab("log10 Normalized Counts") +
    ggtitle("Top 20 Significant DE Genes") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
  ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "pairwise",
                   paste0(clusters[x], "_",
                          levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[A], "_vs_",
                          levels(cluster_metadata$group_id)[B],
                          "_top20_DE_genes.png")))
}

Upstream calls this with a bare map(), which aborts the whole sweep at the first cluster that fails. Small clusters such as Megakaryocytes can easily fail, so we wrap each call so that one failure does not hide the other seven.

# Run the script on all clusters comparing stim condition relative to control
# condition
wald_outcomes <- map(1:length(clusters),
                     function(i) {
                       tryCatch(get_dds_resultsAvsB(i, A = 2, B = 1),
                                error = function(e) {
                                  message("Cluster ", clusters[i], " failed: ",
                                          conditionMessage(e))
                                  conditionMessage(e)
                                })
                     })
names(wald_outcomes) <- clusters

Script to run DESeq2 on all cell type clusters, likelihood ratio test

# Likelihood ratio test
dir.create(file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt"), showWarnings = FALSE)

# Create DESeq2Dataset object
clusters <- levels(factor(metadata$cluster_id))

metadata <- gg_df %>%
  dplyr::select(cluster_id, sample_id, group_id)

metadata$group <- paste0(metadata$cluster_id, "_", metadata$group_id) %>%
  factor()
# DESeq2
library(DEGreport)
get_dds_LRTresults <- function(x) {

  cluster_metadata <- metadata[which(metadata$cluster_id == clusters[x]), ]
  rownames(cluster_metadata) <- cluster_metadata$sample_id
  cluster_metadata$group_id <- factor(cluster_metadata$group_id)
  counts <- pb[[clusters[x]]]
  cluster_counts <- data.frame(counts[, which(colnames(counts) %in% rownames(cluster_metadata))])

  # all(rownames(cluster_metadata) == colnames(cluster_counts))

  dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cluster_counts,
                                colData = cluster_metadata,
                                design = ~ group_id)

  dds_lrt <- DESeq(dds, test = "LRT", reduced = ~ 1)

  # Extract results
  res_LRT <- results(dds_lrt)

  # Create a tibble for LRT results
  res_LRT_tb <- res_LRT %>%
    data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>%
    as_tibble()

  # Save all results
  write.csv(res_LRT_tb,
            file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt",
                      paste0(clusters[x], "_LRT_all_genes.csv")),
            quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)

  # Subset to return genes with padj < 0.05
  sigLRT_genes <- res_LRT_tb %>%
    dplyr::filter(padj < 0.05)

  # Save sig results
  write.csv(sigLRT_genes,
            file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt",
                      paste0(clusters[x], "_LRT_sig_genes.csv")),
            quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)

  # Transform counts for data visualization
  rld <- rlog(dds_lrt, blind = TRUE)

  # Extract the rlog matrix from the object and compute pairwise correlation values
  rld_mat <- assay(rld)
  rld_cor <- cor(rld_mat)

  # Obtain rlog values for those significant genes
  cluster_rlog <- rld_mat[sigLRT_genes$gene, ]

  cluster_meta_sig <- cluster_metadata[which(rownames(cluster_metadata) %in% colnames(cluster_rlog)), ]

  # # Remove samples without replicates
  # cluster_rlog <- cluster_rlog[, -1]
  # cluster_metadata <- cluster_metadata[which(rownames(cluster_metadata) %in% colnames(cluster_rlog)), ]

  # Use the `degPatterns` function from the 'DEGreport' package to show gene
  # clusters across sample groups
  cluster_groups <- degPatterns(cluster_rlog, metadata = cluster_meta_sig,
                                time = "group_id", col = NULL)
  ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt",
                   paste0(clusters[x], "_LRT_DEgene_groups.png")))

  # Let's see what is stored in the `df` component
  write.csv(cluster_groups$df,
            file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt",
                      paste0(clusters[x], "_LRT_DEgene_groups.csv")),
            quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)

  saveRDS(cluster_groups,
          file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt",
                    paste0(clusters[x], "_LRT_DEgene_groups.rds")))
  save(dds_lrt, cluster_groups, res_LRT, sigLRT_genes,
       file = file.path(results_dir, "DESeq2", "lrt",
                        paste0(clusters[x], "_all_LRTresults.Rdata")))
}
lrt_outcomes <- map(1:length(clusters),
                    function(i) {
                      tryCatch(get_dds_LRTresults(i),
                               error = function(e) {
                                 message("Cluster ", clusters[i], " failed: ",
                                         conditionMessage(e))
                                 conditionMessage(e)
                               })
                    })
names(lrt_outcomes) <- clusters
Note

The LRT here compares ~ group_id against ~ 1, which with a two-level factor is close to the Wald test above rather than a genuinely multi-group design. The upstream lesson presents it as a template to adapt when there are three or more groups.
